claims.statement: Yoshizawa explicitly targets Metz 2013 chapter 7 and argues that a concern about losing already valuable ordinary life is not captured merely by demanding perfect value.
limitations: This is a developed criticism and reconstruction, not his endorsement of immortality as necessary.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa distinguishes the person possessing meaning-making properties from the life assessed, and separates whole/part life, time and pro tanto/on-balance meaning.
limitations: A proposed philosophical framework; neither its categories nor its monopolar preference are established facts.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa distinguishes an existing person without meaning-making properties from there being no such person; he rejects inferring general meaninglessness from the latter.
limitations: He allows particular deaths to prevent achievements; his rejection is not the claim that death never matters.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa ultimately rejects the general claim that a person’s death itself makes her life meaningless and favours naturalistic objectivism.
limitations: Attribution only; his conclusion is philosophically disputed and does not establish naturalism about consciousness.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa allows continuity, posthumous events and others’ survival to matter, while distinguishing this from a general final-loss nihilism.
limitations: An argument about the value and temporal status of lives does not establish actual further first-person experience.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa expressly does not certify that Tolstoy intended his reconstruction of the final-loss rationale.
limitations: Metz 2015 p253 describes it as the best way to understand Tolstoy; neither author supplies a fresh full historical-source inspection here.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa identifies his 2011 Japanese paper as principally addressing Metz 2003, and his 2015 paper as a developed treatment of Metz 2013.
limitations: Neither the Japanese original nor Metz 2003 has been inspected in this packet.

claims.statement: Metz’s actual 2015 reply grants the distinction between absent perfect value and losing imperfect value, and grants that the latter deserves attention.
limitations: Concession of an omitted rationale does not concede its soundness.

claims.statement: Metz objects that calling the ended life already meaningful concedes meaning without immortality; he proposes instead a rationale under which the ending is what makes the life meaningless.
limitations: This targets a strict necessity formulation; neither formulation proves a finite life valueless.

claims.statement: Metz questions whether endlessly retained love or contemplation would still be merely ordinary value, and considers a possible distinction between perfection and what explains meaninglessness.
limitations: The suggested response on Yoshizawa’s behalf is hypothetical, not an inspected later publication. The explanatory bridge remains contested.

claims.statement: Metz separates the individual or species assessed from whether the source of meaning is natural or supernatural; his individual-life inquiry does not simply exclude supernatural sources by definition.
limitations: Only declared part of §2.1 read; Tartaglia’s original and the rest of this reply remain uninspected.

claims.statement: Metz’s 2015 discussion concedes he did not conclusively establish either an incompatibility of divine atemporality with purposiveness or that only his preferred qualitative divine properties could ground meaning.
limitations: Partial §3.2 extent; Poettcker’s original is not independently inspected. This is not a retroactive rewording of Metz 2000.

claims.statement: Wolf’s final 2010 first lecture treats meaningfulness as a distinctive value involving fitting concern and positive engagement with independently worthy objects.
limitations: The final book version is newly inspected; no claim of textual identity with the v1 draft or proof of objective value.

claims.statement: Wolf argues that feeling fulfilled or producing benefits incidentally does not alone supply the fitting engagement required by her account.
limitations: Counterexamples are philosophical illustrations; no clinical findings about drugs, mental illness or well-being are established.

claims.statement: Wolf’s final first lecture explicitly limits what its qualitative account offers a person distressed by cosmic smallness or inability to make a large lasting impact.
limitations: It offers possible solace, not a comprehensive solution to every ultimate-context concern.

claims.statement: Wolf ends the selected first lecture by declining to promise a theory of objective value or an infallible identification procedure.
limitations: The second lecture, comments and response are not inspected; this is not a whole-book rejection or resolution of value grounding.

claims.statement: Fischer’s inspected reprint distinguishes the identity condition from the attractiveness of a future life to the present person.
limitations: A stipulated future bearer is not evidence of actual survival; this is his reconstruction of Williams, whose original is inherited here.

claims.statement: Fischer distinguishes outwardly absorbed experiential content from ownership of experience, rejecting an automatic inference from the former to loss of the subject.
limitations: This blocks one inference; it does not supply a complete criterion of numerical identity.

claims.statement: Fischer argues that an appealing endless life could contain varied activities and periods of boredom; it need not be one uniformly absorbing activity.
limitations: Possibility argument and standards comparison, not a proof that compulsory endless life is desirable.

claims.statement: Fischer distinguishes self-exhausting from repeatable pleasures, relative to a person and their distribution, and proposes that repeatable goods may sustain categorical desires.
limitations: Extrapolation to unending life and the relation of pleasure to meaning remain contestable; no measured immortal sample.

claims.statement: Fischer permits changes of character arising through appropriate reflection to remain attractive, while distinguishing coercion, deception and other unwelcome changes.
limitations: Finite analogies do not resolve every indefinitely extended identity or present-concern case.

claims.statement: The inspected Fischer review copy is a later reprint layout, not the 1994 journal layout: its pages are224–238 and its apparatus includes an editorial 1996 publication note and a 2004 translation.
source_locators: p. 225 n. 11; p238references; primary 1994 metadata Q012R001; Broadview metadata Q008R001
limitations: Broadview 2009 anthology is a supported candidate; exact proof-to-final and journal collation remains unresolved. PDF 2022 dates do not date the argument.

claims.statement: The selected final-loss exchange does not establish that ending a life erases its earlier value; treating absence as an existing state without meaning requires a further bridge.
limitations: The strongest strict necessity advocate can dispute retrospective attribution; the present packet does not settle every theory of value or time.

claims.statement: Possible worthwhile continuation requires relevant goods, an appropriate relation to the person, and actual further experience before it can support a personal-survival claim.
limitations: Information, recognition and a complete history can preserve something valuable without supplying further subjectivity. No new empirical survival evidence.

claims.statement: An occurrence of consciousness, an intended role, and a worthy role remain distinct claims; duration or value alone establishes none of the agency, intention and normative bridges.
limitations: No creator purpose, goodness, authority or metaphysical family winner is established.

claims.statement: Yoshizawa explicitly distinguishes the four-dimensional existence of a finite life from eternity or transcending temporality.
limitations: His Singer quotation is not an independent inspection of Singer; neither eternalism nor a timeless conscious bearer is established.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 defines purpose theory as a conditional account of what could confer meaning, not a claim that God or an assigned purpose actually exists. It can permit meaning without an afterlife.
limitations: Purpose theory is distinct from justice/perfection theories; no existence or survival inference.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 distinguishes a purpose assigned from a purpose fulfilled, and separates the grounding account from epistemic knowledge of which purpose or how to fulfil it.
limitations: Unknown guidance does not by itself refute the conditional theory, but no actual purpose is verified.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 argues that some versions of purpose theory can avoid the disrespect objection by making a respectful request for free moral action rather than manipulation.
limitations: This relies on contested Kantian/retributive/autonomy premises; the article rejects an infinite-damnation version atp298. No theodicy or punishment practice is justified by this packet.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 frames his principal objection around God’s being necessary for any meaning, and explicitly distinguishes that thesis from God’s possible enhancement of meaningful lives.
limitations: His historical and sociological generalizations about what most religious thinkers or naturalists accept are not independently verified.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 proposes that uniquely valuable divine qualitative properties best explain strict divine necessity, while arguing those properties prima facie conflict with purposiveness.
limitations: The value of unity/independence and the characterization of divine agency are argued sketches. The claim does not refute every divine concept or all possible nonpurposive grounding.

claims.statement: Metz 2000 explicitly says his stated objection does not require disbelief in purpose theory and presents compatibility and alternative-grounding reply strategies.
limitations: This qualification is present in the 2000 original; the 2015 caveats cannot be treated as proof of a new wholesale retraction. Referenced Stump/Kretzmann, Rogers and Lodzinski bodies are not inspected for this packet.

arguments.name: Final loss and the necessity of endurance
arguments.position: Reconstructed strict necessity rationale; neither Yoshizawa nor Metz endorses its soundness
premises: Ordinary relationships and activities can be valuable.
Death ends a person and may end valued relationships.
The strict advocate claims the ending makes the whole life meaningless.
bridge_principles: Ending must negate relevant whole-life significance, not merely preclude additional goods.
The meaning at issue and its temporal bearer must be specified.
arguments.conclusion: The third premise would require endurance for meaning only if the loss-to-meaninglessness bridge is defended.
arguments.strongest_objection: Yoshizawa distinguishes no existing subject from an existing subject without meaning, and past meaning from present instantiation; strict necessity does not follow from an ending.
arguments.strongest_reply: Metz reformulates the strict rationale to avoid conceding finite meaning, then questions whether endless retention avoids ideal value; his hypothetical further response separates perfection from explanatory work.
unresolved_issues: The selected 2013 original remains unavailable. No later author summary or critic replaces that missing inspection.
Yoshizawa’s Tolstoy reconstruction is not verified historical intention.
Final-loss concern is neither merely boredom nor settled by labelling the desired good perfect.

arguments.name: Possible worthwhile continuation with ownership and engagement
premises: Some activities can remain worthwhile or repeatable.
A future life can contain varied goods and changes acceptable through reflection.
The future experiences must belong to the same person and remain appropriately attractive.
bridge_principles: Finite repeatability must extend to the proposed duration.
Future subjectivity and identity must actually obtain for survival.
Possible appeal does not establish all endless lives good.
arguments.conclusion: A coherent worthwhile continuation may enhance a life, while finite meaning and actual survival remain separate questions.
arguments.strongest_objection: Williams’s stronger concern is exhausted categorical projects or a remote life not appropriately related to the present person; ordinary repetition may fail indefinitely.
arguments.strongest_reply: Fischer distinguishes repeatable from self-exhausting goods, permits a varied life and appropriate character changes, and separates absorption from ownership.
unresolved_issues: Williams original is frozen accepted derivative, not fresh reading.
No infinite aggregate-value measure, empirical immortality or survival inference.
Fischer exact proof-to-final and journal collation unresolved.

arguments.name: Finite value, ultimate context and intended purpose
arguments.position: Several conditional questions; no forced metaphysical winner
premises: Worthwhile engagement can be evaluated at the level of an individual life.
Cosmic role or ultimate context asks additional questions.
Intended purpose requires agency/end/grounding; worthwhile purpose requires normative justification.
bridge_principles: Local worth must not silently become an answer to every ultimate-context concern.
Descriptive occurrence must not become intention.
A divine theory’s possibility is distinct from its actuality or necessity.
arguments.conclusion: Finite value and possible divine/enduring enhancement can be compared without deriving purpose, perfect goodness or actual continuation.
arguments.strongest_objection: An advocate may argue all finite value requires divine grounding or that ultimate loss defeats local significance.
arguments.strongest_reply: Wolf identifies finite fitting engagement but expressly limits cosmic solace; Metz concedes limited force of his timeless-purpose challenge in the 2015 selectedpassage. The 2000 original itself already leaves two response strategies open and does not claim the objection requires disbelief (p311).
unresolved_issues: Metz 2000 exact original repaired; direct 2007 Affolter/Metzreply bodies remain deferred. Exact 2013 selectedchapter unavailable.
Affolter 2007 and Poettckeroriginals deferred; no fabricateddirectreplycoverage.
Objectivevaluegrounding, humanidentity and timelessmind remain unresolved.
